extraReferences.title: Diversity and evolution of optically complex eyes in a family of deep-sea fish: ocular diverticula in barreleye spookfish (Opisthoproctidae). Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 10: 1044565
extraReferences.authors: Wagner H.-J., Genner M.J., Partridge J.C. et al.

extraReferences.title: MBARI researchers film rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish in 4K

anatomy.lede: The barreleye is a small, dark fish built around its eyes: two green-lensed tubes inside a clear, fluid-filled dome.

hotspots.label: Transparent shield
hotspots.text: A tough, flexible, see-through skin covers the top of the head. It attaches to the scales behind the head and to clear bones that protect the eyes from the side.

hotspots.label: Tubular eye
hotspots.text: The tubular eyes sit in a fluid-filled chamber under the shield and can rotate through an arc of about 75 degrees, from looking up to looking forward.

hotspots.label: Small mouth
hotspots.text: Its name means 'large fins, small mouth'. The small, pointed mouth suggests it picks out prey precisely.

hotspots.label: Broad fins
hotspots.text: Large, flat fins let it hang nearly motionless and manoeuvre with precision.

hotspots.label: Dorsal fin
hotspots.text: The dorsal fin has 11 soft rays and no spines.

hotspots.label: Dark body
hotspots.text: Adults are dark brown. Their digestive system is large, suggesting they can eat both small drifting animals and jellies.

senses.lede: In the twilight zone, the last of the sunlight comes from straight above, and the barreleye's senses are tuned to it.

senses.name: Light-gathering eyes
senses.text: The tubular shape concentrates light, letting the fish see the silhouettes of prey against the faint sunlight from above. The trade-off, in tubular eyes generally, is a very narrow field of view.

senses.name: Green filters
senses.text: Green pigment in the lenses may filter out direct sunlight, helping the fish tell it apart from the bioluminescent glow of prey overhead.

senses.name: Eyes that look sideways too?
senses.text: Other barreleyes in its family have light-sensitive pouches on their eyes that extend their view to the sides and below. The barreleye's own eyes have so far had only a preliminary description.

senses.name: Smell
senses.text: The two spots above the mouth that look like eyes are actually its nares, olfactory organs comparable to our nostrils.

body.lede: Two features set this fish apart: a head you can see through, and eyes that are not fixed in place.

systems.title: A fluid-filled dome
systems.text: The eyes sit in a chamber of fluid under the clear shield. This fragile structure was missing from older descriptions, probably because it was destroyed when fish were hauled up in nets.

systems.title: Two ways to feed
systems.text: It can either tilt its whole body upwards while keeping its eyes locked on a target, or stay level and roll its eyes forward as food sinks towards its mouth.

mind.lede: Almost everything known about how the barreleye lives comes from a few encounters with underwater robots.

studies.title: Watching the eyes turn
studies.text: ROV video off central California, at 600 to 800 m, showed barreleyes hanging still with eyes glowing green in the lights. A net-caught fish kept alive for several hours on board confirmed that it rotated its eyes as it turned its body upright.

studies.title: A working hypothesis
studies.text: The researchers proposed that the fish waits horizontally with eyes up, then rotates its eyes forward and swims upwards when it spots prey such as a drifting jelly.

studies.title: A rare sighting in 4K
studies.text: A barreleye filmed about 600 m down, roughly 90 km off California, was only MBARI's eleventh observation of the species. The team spent about 20 minutes filming it, testing different lighting to show off its clear head.
